title: Presentation and use of market research results
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Analyse market research data shown in tables and diagrams, and draw simple conclusions from such data.

blocks.heading: Reading a diagram of results
blocks.text:
Analysing market research data means comparing the numbers against each other before saying anything about them: which bar is tallest, which line fell, by how much, and against what. A reading that names the pattern - "mango was chosen by 96 of 200 shoppers, ahead of every rival flavour" - is analysis; a number copied out alone is not.

A conclusion then says what the pattern means for the business: which product to back, which price looks accepted, which group to target. A sound conclusion compares at least two figures, states its size, and stays inside what the data shows. "Mango is the most popular flavour" is a conclusion the table supports; "because mango reminds people of home" is a guess the table cannot prove, because the figures counted choices, not reasons.

blocks.heading: A worked reading
blocks.text: Oshakati Smoothies asked 200 shoppers which flavour they would buy next month. The diagram of results: mango 96, guava 52, baobab 32, no purchase 20. Reading: mango drew 96 of the 200, which is 48 per cent, ahead of guava on 52 and baobab on 32, and the three flavours together accounted for 180 of the 200 asked. Conclusion: mango is the flavour to feature at launch, chosen by close to half the shoppers, while baobab stays a secondary option rather than a headline; the one in ten who would buy none is a reminder that promotion still matters. A Dutch bike-share firm read its rider survey the same way, and built its campaign around the annual pass its table showed commuters preferred.

blocks.heading: Where this skill goes next
blocks.text: The same reading skill - compare, size the pattern, conclude inside the data - carries into topic 3.3, where research results shape price and promotion choices, and into the longer examination questions, where a table or diagram is often the evidence an answer must use. This worked example is the pattern to practise.
